title: Good People Like to Help Good People
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece reframes asking for help as an underused relationship-building tool, especially in new relationships. While big favors early on can backfire, the author argues that small requests, particularly for advice, perspective, or a chance to learn from someone's expertise, tend to flatter the other person and deepen connection rather than harm it. Invitations to speak, attend, or teach are framed as signals of importance that people respond to warmly, provided the request is sincere. The article closes by noting that most people are fundamentally good and want to help other good people, making sincere requests for help a genuine relationship intensifier.
points: Small requests for advice or perspective can deepen a new relationship rather than damage it.
Big, imposing requests early in a relationship are more likely to backfire.
Asking someone to teach you something they know is a larger but often welcomed request.
Sincerity is essential; requests made purely to manufacture goodwill tend to backfire.
Most people hold positive values and want to help others, even relative strangers.
quotes: When attempting to foster a deeper and more meaningful connection in a new relationship, asking for help is underrated.
It takes an impertinent and rude person to ask for something large in a new relationship.
Good people like to help good people, and it is flattering when others, even those they don’t know very well yet, ask for their help with a viewpoint or suggestion.
A somewhat larger request that can foster a deeper connection is to ask others to teach you something they know.
The idea you want to learn from this person and would do anything for that chance acts like a magnet to attract positive affect.
Asking people for help is a relationship intensifier. If the request for help is sincere, everyone wins.
